title: images: Opacity problem with Resize + Padding with PNG output

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the same root cause. Hex color strings are parsed into `color.RGBA`, which Go treats as alpha-premultiplied. A transparent color like `#00f7` (B=0xff > A=0x77) is therefore an invalid premultiplied value and gets corrupted when drawn onto a PNG/RGBA destination. Both switch `hexStringToColorGo` to return `color.NRGBA` for transparent colors, and both make `ColorGoToHexString` and the luminance calculation read the non-premultiplied channels. Both regenerate the same `padding-transparent-chained.png` golden, so on the reported Resize + Padding + PNG scenario they are equivalent in correctness.

The differences are in scope, risk and tests.

Patch B bundles a separate behavioral change in `resources/image.go`. It skips source-palette clamping for every Filter action on paletted PNGs, which its own comment attributes to a different problem. This changes output for all filters on indexed PNGs: they no longer stay paletted, so file sizes and appearance change. It also required regenerating the `overlay.png` and `text.png` goldens. That is unrelated to the padding-opacity issue and adds regression risk.

Patch B also normalizes every `Color` to NRGBA inside `init()` and reworks `AddColorToPalette` equality. These are broader edits that ripple into palette handling. It also rewrites an existing test expectation (`color.RGBA{...,A:0x80}` -> `color.NRGBA`) instead of only adding coverage.

Patch A is minimal. It returns plain `RGBA` for opaque colors, preserving existing behavior, and `NRGBA` only for transparent ones. Its small `colorGoToRGBA8` helper is used consistently for hex output and luminance.

Patch A's tests are much stronger:
- Unit tests for parsing and hex round-tripping of transparent colors.
- A filter test checking padding and text draw identically onto premultiplied and non-premultiplied destinations.
- An end-to-end integration test that resizes to PNG, pads with `#00f7` and decodes the published file to assert the exact NRGBA pixel. This directly reproduces the issue scenario.

Patch B adds only a couple of parse-table entries and relies on golden images.

With equal core correctness, Patch A wins on its targeted scope, lower risk and substantially better tests.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)?

```console
$ hugo version
hugo v0.126.1+extended linux/amd64
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes.

### Report

The [`images.Padding`](https://gohugo.io/functions/images/padding/) function currently ignores the transparency setting when padding a PNG image. While the documentation does state '*conversion to WEBP is required to support transparency*' (under [Other recipes](https://gohugo.io/functions/images/padding/#other-recipes)), I can't see a reason why PNG shouldn't be supported, given that it has an alpha channel. For the moment I have resorted to first converting the image to WEBP, then applying transparent padding, and then converting it back to PNG, but this does not feel like an elegant solution.

title: resources/images: Poor overlay quality when background image is an indexed (not true color) PNG

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix. In `doWithImageConfig` they skip re-applying the source palette when the action is a filter. That addresses the root cause: overlay and text output gets clamped back to the indexed PNG's palette. Both also update the paletted overlay and text golden images in the same way.

Patch A also changes how colors are handled across the board. Hex colors now parse to NRGBA instead of RGBA, `Color.init` normalizes to NRGBA, `ColorGoToHexString` un-premultiplies, and `AddColorToPalette` compares by color value. It also edits existing test expectations and changes the `padding-transparent-chained.png` golden file. These changes target a different issue (12536, premultiplied alpha) and are not needed to fix this one. They alter behavior visible to users, such as how hex strings are interpreted and how colors compare, which adds risk and makes the fix harder to see.

Patch B keeps to the issue. It also adds a focused integration test that checks three things: resize still keeps the palette, overlays (including on a resized image) reproduce the overlay's pixel colors exactly and are not paletted, and the text color survives. This test would fail before the fix and pass after it. Patch A adds no new test for the overlay behavior beyond the golden-file updates.

On correctness the two are equal. Patch B is better on tests and scope.

title: metrics: --templateMetrics duration columns have inconsistent formatting

judge.reasoning:
Both patches replace `time.Duration.String()` with a two-decimal formatter whose unit suffix has a fixed width. Since fmt pads by rune count, both make decimal points line up in right-aligned columns, so both fix the core issue.

Correctness: Patch A handles the rounding edge case. It moves to the next unit when the rounded value reaches 1000, so 999.996µs prints as 1.00ms rather than 1000.00µs, and it handles negative values. Patch B switches on the raw threshold, so it can print values like "1000.00 µs". Alignment still holds in that case, but the output is less tidy. Patch B's space between value and unit broke the existing duration-stripping regex in the partials integration test, and it correctly updated that test. Patch A's format ("1.23s ", "2.00ms") still matches the old regex, so no change was needed. Neither approach is wrong, but A's output stays compatible with existing consumers. One caveat: A relies on `strconv` and `math` already being imported in metrics.go, which I believe they are. A also detects the unit by round-tripping through ParseFloat, which is slightly clunky.

Tests: Patch A tests `formatDuration` thoroughly, including unit boundaries, rounding rollover and negatives. It also adds an end-to-end `WriteMetrics` test that checks decimal-point positions match across rows in both the hints and non-hints modes, which tests the issue's actual requirement. Patch B only unit-tests four representative values and never checks table alignment.

Scope and craft: both are focused. Patch B's code is simpler, but Patch A's edge-case handling and much stronger verification of the alignment property make it the better fix overall.

issue_md:
The `--templateMetrics` output table prints duration values (sum/avg/max) using `time.Duration.String()`, which varies both units and decimal places depending on the magnitude. This makes the table hard to scan when rows have durations of different magnitudes.

**Proposed fix:** Use a fixed-decimal formatter (two decimal places, unit suffix padded to consistent width) so decimal points align across all rows in the table.

title: hugolib: Throw error when Render method is unable to find specified template

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the same root cause. They replace the silent `return "", nil` in `pageContentOutput.Render` with an error when the named layout cannot be found. Both also correct the same malformed `-- layouts/myview.html` txtar header in `tpl/page`. That header fix matters: once missing views raise an error, the broken header would make the existing test fail.

Correctness is equivalent at the core. Patch B's error is more useful, though. It goes through `pco.po.p.wrapError`, the page's existing error-wrapping helper used elsewhere in hugolib, so the message carries page/file context. The text (`failed to resolve layout "view_bar" for .Render: template not found`) also says which call failed. Patch A gives a bare `template "view_bar" not found` with no page context, which is less helpful on a site with many pages.

Tests: Patch A adds only the issue's reproduction and checks the message with a regex. Patch B adds that same case, plus `.Render` on regular pages in a range loop (a different call path), plus a positive check that an existing view still renders correctly. B's tests cover more and would catch regressions in both directions.

Scope: both are minimal, with no unrelated churn. Overall B is better on craft (contextual error, consistent with hugolib conventions) and on test thoroughness.

issue_md:

title: Add  encoding.HexDecode/Encode

judge.reasoning: The production code is functionally identical in both patches: `HexDecode` and `HexEncode` on the encoding namespace use `cast.ToStringE` plus `encoding/hex`, with the same method mappings and examples in `init.go`. Correctness is therefore equal, and the difference comes down to tests and craft. Patch B's unit tests are more thorough. They cover uppercase hex input, empty strings, invalid characters (`zz`), odd-length input (`486`), non-string input (42), and a round-trip check that encoding then decoding reproduces the original. Patch A's unit tests have only one happy-path case and one type-error case per function. Both patches add an integration test that checks the issue's motivating case: building an SRI string with `crypto.SHA256 | encoding.HexDecode | encoding.Base64Encode` and comparing it to the `Data.Integrity` of a fingerprinted resource. Patch B puts this test in a new `encoding_integration_test.go` next to the feature it exercises, and it also checks plain encode and decode output. Patch A puts its test in `tpl/templates/decorator_integration_test.go`, which is an odd place unrelated to the encoding package, and it pulls in decorator, Store and CSP-header machinery that obscures what the test is for. Patch B also adds documentation pages for both functions, including the SRI use case. That earns little credit on its own but adds no risk. Overall, Patch B has stronger edge-case tests and better-placed integration tests for the same implementation.

issue_md:
See https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/15060#issuecomment-4790405347

It's clumsy that you need to create a resource (making up an unique filename) to get a SRI hash.

I suggest we add `crypto.Fingerprint` with a similar signature to https://gohugo.io/functions/resources/fingerprint/

>hash.Fingerprint [ALGORITHM] any -> string

The function name is a little clumsy, but we need to keep the two very similar functions in line.

Where `any` typically is a `string` (but can also be a `Resource` -- we have similar unwrappers elsewhere).

It would then return e.g. `sha256-Yuh...rfE=`.

Note to implementer: There's some obvious code reuse potential here.

title: Make .Render take additional data
issue_md:
See https://gohugo.io/methods/page/render/#article
See #15076

> PAGE.Render NAME

This has been discussed before. 

* The contract has always been that the templates that `.Renders` gets the data context as e.g. `page.html`, a `page.Page`.
* We can only pass 1 argument to Go's template renderer, which I guess is the blocking reason for not having done this sooner.

So, if we want to do:

> PAGE.Render [DATA] NAME

I'm guessing we have 2 top-level options:

* We say that if `DATA` is set, we use that as the context passed to the templates,. else `PAGE`.
* We somehow (e.g. by embeding it in a `{ DataAdditionalContext, Page }` struct or  putting it into the current `context.Context`) wrap the `Page` so you can do both `.RelPermalink` and `.DataAdditionalContext` (naming of the latter is just picked out of a hat without thinking too hard.

+// parseRenderArgs parses the arguments to Page.Render, which are the layout name
+// and an optional data context, i.e. NAME [DATA].
+// For convenience, DATA NAME is also accepted if DATA is not a string.
+func parseRenderArgs(args []any) (layout string, data any, hasData bool, err error) {
+	switch len(args) {
+	case 0:
+		return "", nil, false, errors.New("no layout given")
+	case 1:
+		layout, err = cast.ToStringE(args[0])
+	case 2:
+		nameArg, dataArg := args[0], args[1]
+		isStringKind := func(v any) bool {
+			return v != nil && reflect.TypeOf(v).Kind() == reflect.String
+		}
+		// Use the kind and not the type so e.g. template.HTML names are not swapped.
+		if !isStringKind(nameArg) && isStringKind(dataArg) {
+			// DATA NAME.
+			nameArg, dataArg = dataArg, nameArg
+		}
+		layout, err = cast.ToStringE(nameArg)
+		data, hasData = dataArg, true
+	default:
+		return "", nil, false, fmt.Errorf("too many arguments: expected a layout name and an optional data context, got %d arguments", len(args))
+	}
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", nil, false, fmt.Errorf("invalid layout name: %w", err)
+	}
+	if layout == "" {
+		return "", nil, false, errors.New("no layout given")
+	}
+	return layout, data, hasData, nil
+}

title: New content command thinks there's a path conflict for a file that doesn't exist yet

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix: the placeholder file now sets `draft: false`. In Hugo, a page's own front matter overrides cascaded values. So the cascaded `draft: true` from `posts/drafts/_index.md` no longer drops the placeholder page from the build, and the 'no page found / target path conflicts' error goes away. The placeholder's explicit `build:` block already overrides the cascaded `build.render: link`, so draft was the root cause, and both patches fix it.

Correctness: the two are equivalent for the reported scenario. Patch B also sets `BuildExpired` in the `new content` command, next to the existing `BuildFuture`. This covers the parallel case where a cascaded past `expiryDate` would likewise remove the placeholder. It is a small, low-risk change that matches the existing BuildFuture handling, and the code comments explain why each case is handled where it is.

Tests: both add a Go unit test reproducing the issue's `_index.md` cascade, and both tests would fail before the fix. Patch A tests only the leaf-bundle path. Patch B's unit test covers both the leaf bundle and a regular page, and asserts the placeholder text is gone. B also adds an end-to-end testscript through the actual CLI that covers:
- bundles with a custom kind;
- expired-cascade and future-cascade sections;
- a regular `hugo` build still not publishing the drafts, which guards against the fix leaking drafts into output.
That is much stronger evidence.

Scope and craft: B's extra work is tightly related and well commented, and it adds little risk. A is minimal and clean but less thoroughly verified. Overall, B is the better patch.

I have section called `posts/drafts/` where I create drafts for posts before I move them to a `posts/YEAR/MONTH` directory where I can post them. The bug happens when I create the page for a post, like this: 
hugo new content posts/drafts/trip-to-puebla/index.md

title: hugo --gc deletes in-use image cache files when on-disk path case differs from the cache key (case-insensitive filesystems)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause: the case-sensitive `seen.Has(name)` check in the pruner. They do it in different ways.

Patch A matches the walked name against a lowercased index of the seen keys. A name that differs from a used key only in case becomes a candidate, and the decision waits until the walk finishes. The candidate is removed only if the exact-case key was also walked, which proves the two are distinct files on a case-sensitive filesystem. Otherwise it is kept, because on a case-insensitive filesystem it is the same file the build read. This gives the right answer on both kinds of filesystem without asking the filesystem anything. There are no side effects, no extra I/O and no failure modes. The existing semantics for expired or forced removal are preserved: candidates are only considered when `!shouldRemove`, and an exact-seen file still follows the expiry logic. Error handling is consolidated cleanly into a `remove` helper.

Patch B detects case-insensitivity at runtime by creating, stat-ing and deleting a probe file in the user's cache root in the middle of the prune walk. That writes into the directory being walked and adds an I/O failure path. On probe failure it defaults to case-insensitive matching, which can keep stale entries on case-sensitive filesystems. It is workable but more fragile and intrusive than A's deterministic approach.

Tests: Patch B's simulated case-insensitive afero wrapper is a real strength. Its test runs on every platform and also checks that an unrelated unused entry is still pruned. Patch A tests a real case-insensitive filesystem, which is skipped on Linux, and an end-to-end `hugo --gc` testscript reproducing the issue's scenario, also skipped on Linux. It also adds a MemMapFs case-sensitive test that runs everywhere and confirms distinct-case files are still pruned. A's tests are closer to the real bug, while B's run in more places. On balance this is roughly even. A's additions to `main_test.go` (a testscript condition and a `base64decode` command) exist only to support its testscript, so they are not unrelated churn.

Overall, Patch A's fix is more robust and has no side effects, which outweighs B's portability advantage in testing.

issue_md: ### What happens On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS APFS, Windows), `hugo --gc` deletes image cache files under `resources/_gen` that the build **actively uses**, if the on-disk path case differs from the cache key. The build itself works fine (the case-insensitive filesystem resolves the read), but the pruner's usage check is a case-sensitive string comparison, so the just-used file is considered unused and removed. The relevant code is in `cache/filecache/filecache_pruner.go` (unchanged on master): ```go if !shouldRemove && c.entryLocker.seen.Len() > 0 { // Remove it if it's not been touched/used in the last build. shouldRemove = !c.entryLocker.seen.Has(name) } ``` `seen` contains the cache key (for images: the lowercased target path, via `ImageCache.getOrCreate` → `c.fcache.ReadOrCreate(relTargetPath, …)`), while `name` is the real on-disk name from the filesystem walk. If they differ only in case, `seen.Has(name)` is false and the file is deleted. ### Why the case can differ in practice Page paths have been lowercased since the v0.123 page-system rewrite, so cache keys for page-bundle images are lowercase. Caches created by older Hugo versions preserve the source directory case (e.g. `resources/_gen/images/collections/PastFuture/…`). Such caches are common in the wild: committed to git for CI cold-start speed, restored by CI cache plugins, or simply carried forward on a developer machine across Hugo upgrades. The result is a permanent rebuild/evict cycle: `--gc` deletes the in-use entries → the next build silently re-processes all of them → the new files land inside the surviving mixed-case directory (the prune walk visits directories before deleting their files, so the directory is never seen empty and survives; on a case-insensitive filesystem the re-created file then lands in it) → the next `--gc` deletes them again. On the real site where we found this, every build re-scaled 267 images (~35 s per build, forever). ### Minimal reproduction (macOS) ```sh hugo new site repro && cd repro mkdir -p content/MyBundle layouts/_default printf 'baseURL = "https://example.org/"\ndisableKinds = ["taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap"]\n' > hugo.toml printf -- '---\ntitle: My Bundle\n---\n' > content/MyBundle/index.md cp /path/to/any.jpeg content/MyBundle/cover.jpeg printf '{{ with .Resources.GetMatch "cover.jpeg" }}{{ with .Resize "100x" }}{{ end }}{{ end }}' > layouts/_default/single.html printf 'home' > layouts/_default/home.html hugo # creates resources/_gen/images/mybundle/cover_hu_.jpeg # simulate a cache written by an older Hugo (or copied from elsewhere): mv resources/_gen/images/mybundle resources/_gen/images/tmp mv resources/_gen/images/tmp resources/_gen/images/MyBundle hugo --gc # build succeeds (16 ms, cache hit), but reports "Cleaned 1" find resources -type f # -> empty: the file the build just used is gone hugo # re-processes the image (474 ms) — and writes it back # into the surviving MyBundle/ dir, so the cycle repeats ``` Observed output of the `--gc` build: ``` Processed images │ 1 Cleaned │ 1 Total in 16 ms ``` A cache file that was read 16 ms earlier is deleted as "not been touched/used in the last build". ### What I expected `--gc` should never delete a cache entry that the same build read. On case-insensitive filesystems the usage check should match the way the filesystem resolved the read — e.g. compare case-insensitively (or normalize walk names against the `seen` set) when the cache filesystem is case-insensitive. Renaming the on-disk entry to the key's case would even self-heal old caches. ### Version ``` hugo v0.164.0+extended+withdeploy darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=Homebrew ``` The pruner code is identical on current master.

title: common/hugo: Include aom, dav1d, and libavif in commands/env output

judge.reasoning:
Patch A adds the three requested dependencies (libavif v1.4.1, aom v3.14.1, dav1d 1.5.3) to GetDependencyListNonGo. It keeps the existing hard-coded pattern, so the change is small and easy to verify. The comment now points to the Makefiles to keep in sync. A unit test asserts the exact formatted strings, and the env testscript checks the exact output lines. Both tests would fail before the change and pass after it.

Patch B moves the version constants into internal/warpc and makes common/hugo import internal/warpc. That adds real risk:
- common/hugo is a low-level package. Importing warpc (wazero runtime, embedded WASM blobs) pulls a heavy dependency into it.
- If anything under warpc's import graph depends on common/hugo, the build breaks with an import cycle.

Patch B also has scope and test problems:
- It adds KaTeX with a version constant (0.16.21) the issue never asked for, and nothing in the diff verifies that version against js/package.json.
- It includes unrelated formatting churn in warpc.go and hugo.go, which obscures the fix.
- Its testscript checks only the module paths, not the versions, so it is weaker than Patch A's.

Patch B's centralization idea has some merit, but it does not actually derive versions from the plugin setup; the constants are still hand-maintained. Patch A is the correct, minimal, and better-tested fix.

title: Add classDark and classLight to css.ChromaStyles and "gen chromastyles" (default dark/light)

judge.reasoning: Correctness is equivalent. Both add ClassDark and ClassLight fields to ChromaStylesOptions. Both default each to "dark"/"light" when empty, wire matching --classDark/--classLight CLI flags in gen.go, and build the prefix from the chosen class. Both rely on the existing dict-to-struct decoding for css.ChromaStyles, so the template path works the same way in each. The difference is in tests. Patch A adds only an integration test with positive assertions for the template function. Patch B adds the same integration test plus negative assertions ("! .light .chroma", "! .dark .chroma"), which confirm the default class is actually replaced rather than added alongside. B also extends the gen_chromastyles_mode testscript to cover the CLI flags the issue explicitly asks for ("gen chromastyles"): custom dark class, custom light class, and no effect without --modeSelector. Patch A leaves the new CLI flags untested. Scope is comparable and minimal in both. On craft, B's per-mode defaulting inside the switch is slightly tidier and its doc comments cross-reference the fields, but this is minor. B wins mainly on more thorough test coverage of both entry points named in the issue.

issue_md:
I argued with @jmooring that it would be very unlikely that e.g. the CSS `dark` class would collide with existing classes in a project. After thinking a little, I still don't think that is a likely issue, but:

1. I suspect there are JS/CSS frameworks with other naming standards for these mode classes (e.g. `theme-dark`)
2. I would be an annoyed Hugo user if I needed to customise this class and had to do ugly string replacements.
3. The cost for us adding these 2 new options is small.

title: resources/jsconfig: Address VS Code linting notice in jsconfig.json

judge.reasoning: Patch A fixes the root cause. The lint fires because path entries in `paths` lack a `./` or `../` prefix when `baseUrl` is unset. Patch A normalizes every generated entry so it is explicitly relative. That turns `"*"` into `"./*"`, keeps the self-mapping that lets bare imports resolve to the assets dir in the editor, and also covers source roots nested under `dir` (e.g. `sub/*`). Those nested roots would trigger the same lint, and Patch B leaves them unfixed. Its test checks a sibling root (`../c/*`), the self root (`./*`) and a nested root (`./sub/*`). That test would fail before the change and pass after. Patch B instead drops the mapping for the current dir entirely. In the issue's exact scenario this makes `Build` return nil, so the self-mapping functionality is removed rather than corrected. It also still emits non-relative paths for nested source roots, and its `root == dir` string equality is brittle against path-form differences. Its test only asserts nil for the single-root case and does not check that the remaining paths are valid relative paths. One minor nit on A: on Windows it uses the OS separator (`.\`), but this matches the existing `filepath.Rel`-based behavior. Overall A is more correct, preserves functionality, and has a stronger test.

title: Remove -embedded from the default exec.allow

judge.reasoning: The issue asks only to remove '-embedded' from the default exec.allow. Patch B does exactly that: it changes the sass regex to '^(dart-)?sass$' and updates the TOML test. It also adds explicit assertions that 'sass' and 'dart-sass' are accepted and 'dart-sass-embedded' and 'sass-embedded' are rejected; the rejection checks would fail before the change and pass after it. B also updates the docs (Babel.md example and docs.yaml) to match the new default. Patch A makes the same sass change but also removes '^tailwindcss$' from the default allow list. That is an unrequested behavior change: every TailwindCSS user would need to add tailwindcss to security.exec.allow, which is a breaking change outside the issue's scope. A has to patch three integration tests with custom security.exec.allow settings just to keep them passing, which shows the regression it introduces. A also leaves the node permissions defaults referencing tailwindcss, which is now inconsistent with its own allow list. A adds no meaningful new test of the -embedded removal beyond the TOML string update. B is correct, narrowly scoped, better tested, and keeps the docs consistent.

title: Panic when deleting a directory in static when server is running

judge.reasoning:
Both patches stop the panic, but Patch A also fixes why static events end up in the partial rebuild.

Patch A has two parts. First, it adds an explicit `ComponentFolderStatic` case to the component switch in `processPartialFileEvents`. This matches the existing `ComponentFolderArchetypes` "ignore" case and removes the panic directly. Second, it rewrites `SourceFilesystem.Contains` to use `ReverseLookup`, which does not stat files. The old version iterated mounts, required `dir.IsDir()`, and did prefix matching. That breaks for deleted directories, since a removed mount no longer reports `IsDir`, and for single-file mounts. In those cases the static syncer did not recognise the event as static, so the event fell through to the partial build and hit the panic. With the new `Contains`, the static syncer can classify and sync deletions correctly, so the removed files also disappear from the published output. That is the behaviour a user actually needs.

Patch A's two testscripts cover deleting a directory mounted into static and a file mounted into static while the server runs, and they assert no stderr output (no panic). These are realistic end-to-end reproductions of the reported scenario.

Patch B filters static components out of the resolved paths before parsing. This avoids the panic but only treats the symptom. If `Contains` still misclassifies a deleted static directory, the event is silently dropped from the build and never reaches the static syncer, so stale files may stay in `public`. It also restructures the loop (preallocated slice to append) more than needed. However, it does not check that deleted static files are removed from the output, and it does not cover mounts.

On correctness at the root cause, Patch A is stronger. Its scope remains focused, with a small and clear change consistent with the surrounding code.

title: Issue with chained resource transformations

judge.reasoning:
Root cause: once the chain has run, `resourceAdapterInner.target` is replaced by the transformed resource. `TransformWithContext` then copies that transformed target but keeps the full transformation list, so the earlier steps (e.g. css.Build) run a second time on output that is already built.

Patch A stores the original untransformed target in a new `sourceTarget` field and always starts new chains from it. This fixes the basic Data-then-fingerprint case, and replaying the full chain from source also keeps cache keys consistent. However, `cloneTo` sets `sourceTarget` to a clone of `r.target`. If the transformation has already been applied, that is the transformed resource, while the full chain is still attached. So `resources.Copy` on an already-triggered resource, followed by another transformation, would re-apply the chain to transformed content: the same class of bug. Patch A's only test is the css.Build/Data.Artifacts/fingerprint scenario.

Patch B tracks an `applied` flag and an `appliedCount`. The `transform` loop skips transformations already applied to the target. `sourceKey` keeps the cache key equal to that of a chain built in one go, and the full chain is kept so `hasTransformationPermalinkHash` stays correct. It also avoids sharing the slice backing array with the previous chain, which is a latent aliasing hazard when appending. Finally, `cloneTo` propagates `applied`, explicitly covering the copy case.

B's tests are broader. They trigger the transformation through Data, Content and RelPermalink, check that the chaining result is identical to the untriggered case, test copy before and after the trigger, and include the css.Build artifacts scenario with output file assertions.

B is more complex, but its added logic is well commented and addresses edge cases A misses. On correctness and test coverage, B is the stronger fix.

title: related: Add option to tokenize headings

judge.reasoning:
Patch A is the better fix, mainly on correctness and scope.

**Correctness**
- **ID matching.** A keeps exact-identifier matching and adds heading-title tokens on top of it. B replaces a heading's identifier with its tokens when `tokenize` is on. Under B, heading IDs are no longer indexed, so explicit `fragments` queries by heading ID (e.g. `Related (dict "fragments" ...)`) stop matching.
- **ApplyFilter.** B puts every tokenized-index FragmentKeyword, including query IDs, into `ff.words`. It then compares those only against title words, so ID-based heading filtering breaks for tokenized indices.
- **Query tokens.** A also tokenizes `opts.Fragments` query strings and deduplicates keywords, so a shared word counts once per document. Its ApplyFilter path still checks IDs first and then title tokens, honouring ToLower.
- **HTML in titles.** A's tokenizer strips HTML tags (heading titles can contain `<code>`) and decodes entities. B's `splitWords` decodes entities but leaves tags in place, so tag fragments can leak into tokens.

**Scope**
- B extends tokenization to basic indices via `ToKeywords`. The issue explicitly limits it to heading titles in fragments indices, and this change also alters keyword query behaviour.
- B adds an unrequested `MinTokenLength` option and makes whitespace churn in existing tests.
- A sticks to the issue's specification and adds the requested documentation text verbatim.

**Tests**
- Both add meaningful tests.
- A's integration test covers default vs. tokenize vs. toLower, applyFilter output, definition terms staying exact, inline code in titles, and query strings.
- A also has unit tests for the tokenizer, keyword generation, config decoding and duplicate-weight avoidance.
- B's tests are reasonable, but several target behaviour outside the issue's scope (basic-index tokenization, minTokenLength).

issue_md:
See <https://discourse.gohugo.io/t/related-posts-based-on-heading/57467>.

I suggest using the name `tokenize`, documented as follows:

> (`bool`) Whether to split multi-word values into individual keywords for indexing and matching. Currently applies to heading titles in indices of type `fragments`; non-heading fragments such as definition terms continue to use exact-identifier matching regardless of this setting. This increases index size in proportion to the average number of words per heading; use `cardinalityThreshold` to prune common words and reduce build time. Default is `false`.

title: ReadingTime and FuzzyWordCount have off-by-one errors in their ceiling calculations

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same production change in hugolib/page__content.go: `(wc+99)/100*100` for FuzzyWordCount, and `(wc+211)/212` and `(wc+499)/500` for ReadingTime. Both fix the root cause, so they tie on correctness. Both add the issue's boundary integration test, which fails before the fix and passes after it. Patch B also covers the zero-word case (p0 → "0|0|0"), which the issue's table lists explicitly (0 → 100 currently, 0 expected). With the new formula an empty page gives fuzzyWordCount 0 and readingTime 0, so the assertion is valid and strengthens coverage. Patch A adds a lot of unrelated churn to page_test.go: purely cosmetic reformatting of many existing `AssertFileContent` and `Assert` calls (16 lines removed). This obscures the diff and adds review noise without functional value. Patch B touches only what the fix needs and places the test next to the related TestWordCount. B wins on tests and on scope.

issue_md:
## Summary

Two related integer-arithmetic bugs in `hugolib/page__content.go` (in the plain-content calculation), causing behavior that deviates from documented intent at boundary values.

## 1. `ReadingTime` divides by 213/501 instead of 212/500

```go
if isCJKLanguage {
    result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 500) / 501
} else {
    result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 212) / 213
}
```

The intent is a reading speed of 212 words per minute (500 for CJK), rounded up. But the correct ceiling-division idiom is `(n + d - 1) / d`. As written, the expression computes `ceil(wordCount / 213)` and `ceil(wordCount / 501)`, so the effective reading speeds are 213 and 501 wpm.

| wordCount | current: `(wc+212)/213` | expected at 212 wpm: `ceil(wc/212)` |
|---|---|---|
| 212 | 1 | 1 |
| 213 | **1** | **2** |
| 424 | 2 | 2 |
| 425 | **2** | **3** |

Proposed fix:

```go
result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 211) / 212   // non-CJK
result.readingTime = (result.wordCount + 499) / 500   // CJK
```

## 2. `FuzzyWordCount` overshoots on exact multiples of 100

```go
result.fuzzyWordCount = (result.wordCount + 100) / 100 * 100
```

Documented as the word count "rounded up to the nearest multiple of 100", but adding 100 unconditionally bumps exact multiples to the *next* multiple:

| wordCount | current | expected |
|---|---|---|
| 99 | 100 | 100 |
| 100 | **200** | **100** |
| 101 | 200 | 200 |
| 0 | **100** | **0** |

Proposed fix:

```go
result.fuzzyWordCount = (result.wordCount + 99) / 100 * 100
```

Both changes only affect output at exact boundary values, but they do change rendered output for existing sites (e.g., a 100-word page's `FuzzyWordCount` drops from 200 to 100), so this may warrant a changelog note.

title: panic: slice bounds out of range in contentNodeShifter.Delete when removing draft pages from a multilingual taxonomy

judge.reasoning:
The two production fixes are essentially identical. Both change the `Delete` and `DeleteFunc` shifter contracts to return an updated node. Both stop mutating the `contentNodes` slice in place while ranging over it, which is the root cause: `append(v[:i], v[i+1:]...)` inside a range shifts elements under the iterator. This corrupts the shared backing array, leaves a stale duplicated tail in the stored value, and later causes the slice-bounds panic. Both then re-insert the updated value into the tree when something was deleted but the node isn't empty. They also handle `DeleteFuncRaw` the same way.

Minor code differences are negligible:
- B preallocates `kept` with `make` and adds a comment explaining why the slice is never modified in place.
- A uses nil-initialised `remaining` and a separate `vv` variable in the default case.

The difference is in the tests.

**Patch A** tests only the shifter in isolation with a hand-rolled fake node type. It checks the returned counts and `updated` values. It never exercises the tree path that actually panicked: repeated `NodeShiftTree.delete` calls on the same key, with the updated value stored back.

**Patch B** tests through the real `NodeShiftTree` with real `resourceSource` nodes:
- It deletes languages sequentially in a non-trivial order, which is the multi-delete scenario that left a stale tail and panicked.
- After each step it verifies the stored raw value's length and identity.
- It checks that repeated deletes are no-ops and that the original slice isn't mutated.
- It covers nested `contentNodesMap` inside `contentNodes`.
- It covers `DeleteFuncRaw` with adjacent and trailing deletions, which is exactly the skip-element bug the old in-place loop had.

These tests reproduce the reported failure mode end-to-end and would fail against the old logic. B's tests are therefore materially stronger and more faithful to the issue, so B wins.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using?

Reproduced on both:

```
hugo v0.159.1-86c7d3afacab79dc53325602d77ef884b7570268+extended darwin/arm64
hugo v0.164.0+extended+withdeploy darwin/arm64
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (0.164.0).

### What did you expect to see?

A production build (no `-D`) of a multilingual site containing draft pages completes.

### What did you see instead?

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [5:4]

goroutine 37 [running]:
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*contentNodeShifter).Delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x...}, {0x2, 0x0, 0x0})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_contentnodeshifter.go:48 +0x5f4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x35})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:165 +0x84
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).Delete(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:107
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages.func1-range1(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:106 +0xa4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:138 +0x168
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*HugoSites).assemble(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/hugo_sites_build.go:345 +0x41c
```

The `0x35` in `delete(..., {…, 0x35})` is 53, exactly the byte length of the key being removed (`/blog/` plus a 47-character slug).

### Only on the page-removal path

`hugo -D` (drafts included) builds fine. The panic appears only when a page is *removed* from the tree, which makes it invisible in local preview and fatal only in production.

A **future `publishDate`** panics identically. Setting `[_build] render = "never"` / `list = "never"` on the same pages avoids it entirely — consistent with those pages never being added to the tree, so nothing is deleted.

### What I ruled out

Site: 8 languages, ~1,490 pages per language, ~11,455 content files, `categories` taxonomy.

- **Not a regression.** 0.159.1 and 0.164.0 behave identically.
- **Not the number of drafts.** 96 draft pages build fine; 16 panic.
- **Not slug length.** The panicking key was 47 chars, but renaming an unrelated post to exactly 47 chars builds fine.
- **Not the slug.** Renaming the offending page does not help.
- **Not byte layout.** Deleting a front-matter line, or adding a blank one, still panics.

Swapping page *content* at a fixed path isolates it to **front matter**. Changing `categories = ["Airport Operations"]` on the offending page to any other value clears the panic — and so does moving a *different* page out of that same category while leaving the offending one alone. So the trigger is combinatorial: some particular set of pages being deleted from one taxonomy term corrupts the shifter, rather than any single page being malformed.

### Reproducer

I have not managed to minimise it, and I want to be upfront about that. Synthetic multilingual sites (8 languages, 12 blog + 200 glossary pages sharing one taxonomy term, varying draft counts) do **not** reproduce, so something else in the real tree is required. The affected repository is private.

I am happy to run patches or instrumented builds against the real site and report back, which may be faster than guessing at a minimal case.

title: Add resources.Publish

judge.reasoning:
Both patches have the same core fix. Each adds a `Namespace.Publish` method that type-asserts to `resource.Source`, calls `Publish()` and returns the original resource. Each registers it through `AddMethodMapping`. So both resolve the issue equally at the root, and `{{ ... | resources.Publish }}` works in both.

B is slightly more robust: it adds an explicit nil check, matching the "must provide a Resource object" convention used elsewhere in that namespace. Its doc comment explains the pipe use case.

On tests, A covers only a single happy path (minify, then publish, file exists). B tests several resource kinds (plain text, a minified transformation, an image, a copied resource, and an unpublished control) and checks the published file content. It also checks that a copied resource is published at its new path and not the original, and that unpublished resources are not written. B adds a negative test showing a non-Source (a Page) fails with the expected error.

B's test has some risk: the copied-resource `Name` assertion and the base64 PNG fixture depend on test-builder behavior. Even so, its coverage is much broader and more meaningful.

B also adds user-facing docs for the new function. This is neutral to slightly positive and adds no risk.

Overall the correctness is equivalent, and B wins on tests and edge-case handling.

+// published) and returns it unchanged, allowing it to be used in a pipe, e.g.
+// {{ resources.Get "main.js" | js.Build | resources.Publish }}.
+func (ns *Namespace) Publish(r resource.Resource) (resource.Resource, error) {
+	if r == nil {
+		return nil, errors.New("must provide a Resource object")
+	}
+	src, ok := r.(resource.Source)
+	if !ok {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%T can not be published", r)

+	}

title: Upgrade to Go 1.27

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core changes: CI images, the GitHub matrix, the Dockerfile, go.mod, the regenerated golden PNGs, and the same template-package sync (the CVE jsCtx brace fix, delimiter-aware parse tree String(), stringer regeneration, Funcs docs, new tests). The difference is in handling Go 1.27 behaviour outside the template packages. Patch B fixes internal/warpc so that ErrShutdown from d.inGroup.Wait() is not treated as an error. Its comment says that since Go 1.27 (json/v2), Decode surfaces the read error from the closed pipes; without this, dispatcher shutdown would return a spurious error under the new toolchain. Patch A leaves this untouched. B also adds a mutex around wazero compilation-cache creation to address a data race. It fixes hugio.CopyDir so the shouldCopy predicate is actually applied to files; previously it was ignored for files. B also makes the fork script robust for the sync step: it preserves the stubbed testenv.go and staticcheck.conf, uses godebug replacers, adds the validateType rename, and modernizes build tags. That reflects the issue's 'Synch template packages' task more completely. Patch A's SkipGoldenTests bump to Go >= 1.27 is a sensible touch, and A has less churn. However, B's test-file churn is a reformat of forked upstream test code toward upstream style: removing `// +build` lines and composite-literal layout. That is low risk, though the multi_test import grouping is a little untidy. The cmp.Or-to-herrors.Or swap and the integrationtest_builder cleanup are neutral. Weighing correctness first, B addresses real Go 1.27 runtime breakage that A misses, so B is the better upgrade.

title: templates.Defer: identical block bodies in different output formats share one escaping mode, chosen non-deterministically per build

judge.reasoning:
Both patches apply the same root-cause fix in `handleWith`. Each folds the owner's `IsPlainText` into the deferred-template hash, so HTML and plain-text owners with byte-identical bodies get distinct IDs and are parsed in their own escaping namespace. Same-format owners still share the ID, which preserves the documented key/content-hash sharing. Patch A uses the prefixes "html:"/"text:" and Patch B uses `fmt.Sprintf("%t:%s")`; both prefix every input unambiguously, so they are functionally equivalent. B relies on `fmt` being imported in `templatetransform.go`, which the diff does not show; that is a minor uncertainty, though `fmt` is likely already present.

The tests are where the patches differ. Each adds the issue's reproduction as a test. That test fails on every pre-fix build, since exactly one output is always wrong, so A's 10-build loop is redundant but harmless. A also adds a second test asserting that identical bodies with the same key across two layouts of the same output format still share one execution (`IN[1]` on both pages). This guards the constraint the issue explicitly calls out, and B does not test it. A's comment also explains the reasoning more fully. A is therefore modestly better on test coverage, with equal correctness.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes. ```text hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio ``` Over one run of 40 consecutive builds of the unchanged reproduction site below with that binary, 28 builds published the wrong value in `public/index.html` and 12 published the wrong value in `public/index.txt`. All 40 exited 0, and none printed a warning or an error. ### Summary When two templates belonging to different output formats contain byte-identical `templates.Defer` block bodies, both blocks do execute, each with its own correct output-format context. What they share is the escaping applied inside the block, and which of the two escaping modes survives changes from build to build of an unchanged site. On every build exactly one of the two outputs is therefore wrong: either an HTML page publishes a value raw that it escapes correctly a few characters earlier outside the block, or a plain-text page receives HTML entities. ### Reproduction Three files in an empty directory. No content, no modules, no external tooling. `hugo.toml`: ```toml baseURL = 'https://example.org/' title = 'defer probe' disableKinds = ['page', 'section', 'taxonomy', 'term', 'RSS', 'sitemap', 'robotsTXT'] [outputFormats.probe] mediaType = 'text/plain' baseName = 'index' isPlainText = true [outputs] home = ['html', 'probe'] ``` `layouts/home.html`: ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `layouts/home.probe.txt`, byte-identical to `layouts/home.html` (both md5 `c921197a9c8637852e38d94a0352359d`): ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `OUT[...]` interpolates the value outside the deferred block, `IN[...]` interpolates the same value inside it. Then run `hugo` several times without changing anything, and look at `public/index.html` and `public/index.txt` after each run. ### What happens Two consecutive runs of the same command on the unchanged site, pasted verbatim: ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 0s INFO build: step process duration 0s INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 1.3703ms INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat probe duration 509.5µs INFO build: step render pages 2 content 0 duration 1.8798ms INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 1.7766ms INFO build: step postProcess duration 0s INFO build: duration 4.171ms │ EN ──────────────────┼──── Pages │ 2 Paginator pages │ 0 Non-page files │ 0 Static files │ 0 Processed images │ 0 Aliases │ 0 Cleaned │ 0 Total in 12 ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[&] ``` ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 513.8µs INFO build: step process duration 513.8µs INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 517.9µs INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat probe duration 517.2µs INFO build: step render pages 2 content 0 duration 1.0351ms INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 2.0736ms INFO build: step postProcess duration 0s INFO build: duration 3.6225ms │ EN ──────────────────┼──── Pages │ 2 Paginator pages │ 0 Non-page files │ 0 Static files │ 0 Processed images │ 0 Aliases │ 0 Cleaned │ 0 Total in 12 ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[<b>&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[<b>&] ``` In the first run the HTML page publishes `&` raw inside the block, a few characters after escaping the same value correctly outside it. In the second run the plain-text page receives `<b>&`. Nothing changed between the two runs. Quantified over builds of the unchanged site, each build a separate one-shot `hugo` invocation: | Hugo version | builds | `index.html` published raw `&` inside the block | `index.txt` published `<b>&` inside the block | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | v0.164.0, fresh copy of the site per build | 40 | 25 | 15 | | v0.164.0, fresh copy of the site per build, second run | 40 | 23 | 17 | | v0.165.0, fresh copy of the site per build | 40 | 26 | 14 | | v0.165.0, fresh copy of the site per build, second run | 40 | 28 | 12 | | v0.164.0, repeated builds in one directory | 12 | 8 | 4 | | v0.165.0, repeated builds in one directory | 8 | 5 | 3 | In all 180 of those builds the two output formats carried the *same* string inside the block, so exactly one of the two published files was wrong every time; outside the block the value was escaped correctly for its format in every build. ### What I expected Each format's deferred block rendered under that format's own escaping — `IN[<b>&]` in `public/index.html` and `IN[&]` in `public/index.txt` — and the same result on every build of an unchanged site. The documentation says "The output format, site, and language will be the same, even if the execution is deferred." The output-format *context* does hold up, as the identity-token control below shows; it is the escaping regime that does not follow the output format. ### Controls All of these were run at both v0.164.0 and v0.165.0. **The block really does execute once per output format.** Adding `{{ warnf "DEFER-EXEC-%d" math.Counter }}` to the start of the still byte-identical block body logs two executions in every build: ```text WARN DEFER-EXEC-1 WARN DEFER-EXEC-2 INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 1.7497ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[&] ``` So this is not one rendering substituted into two files; it is two renderings sharing one escaping mode. **Different `key` values do not separate them.** With `"KH"` in `layouts/home.html` and `"KT"` in `layouts/home.probe.txt`, the block bodies still byte-identical, the escaping stayed shared and kept flipping: 36 builds, 22 with the HTML page wrong and 14 with the plain-text page wrong. **Different block body text does separate them, stably.** Changing the body to `INH[{{ .v }}]` in the HTML template and `INT[{{ .v }}]` in the plain-text template gives the correct per-format result in 36 of 36 builds, with no flip: `INH[<b>&]` in `public/index.html` and `INT[&]` in `public/index.txt`. **The per-format context inside the block is correct.** With the body still byte-identical in both templates, but carrying an output-format identity token next to the value: ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ (index page.AlternativeOutputFormats 0).Name }}|{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` With exactly two formats configured the single alternative names the *other* one, so `IN[probe|...]` marks the execution that produced the HTML page and `IN[html|...]` the one that produced the plain-text page. That token was correct in 36 of 36 builds, while the escaping of the value beside it in the very same body was shared and flipped across those builds: ```text public/index.html OUT[<b>&]IN[probe|&] public/index.txt OUT[&]IN[html|&] public/index.html OUT[<b>&]IN[probe|<b>&] public/index.txt OUT[&]IN[html|<b>&] ``` ### Where this appears to come from Offered as a lead from reading the source, not as an instrumented finding. `tpl/tplimpl/templatetransform.go`, `handleWith` (v0.164.0, function at line 409) registers the extracted block under a hash of the block body alone, at lines 450-459: ```go inner := withNode.List.CopyList() s := inner.String() ... innerHash := hashing.XxHashFromStringHexEncoded(s) deferredID := tpl.HugoDeferredTemplatePrefix + innerHash ... c.deferNodes[deferredID] = inner ``` Nothing about the owning template, its output format or its media type enters that identifier, so two templates in different output formats with the same body produce the same `deferredID`. `tpl/tplimpl/templatestore.go`, `addDeferredTemplate` (v0.164.0, function at line 916) then keeps only the first registration under that name, and the first owner fixes the parse namespace for whoever comes later: ```go if _, found := t.templatesByPath.Get(name); found { return nil } ... if owner.D.IsPlainText { prototype := t.tns.parseText ... } else { prototype := t.tns.parseHTML ... } ``` That is exactly the escaping regime the two output formats disagree about, and the loser silently inherits the winner's. Which owner gets there first looks order-dependent. `transformTemplates` (function at line 1916) reaches the registrations by ranging `s.templates()` at line 1937, and that iterator's inner loop at line 1784 ranges a `map[nodeKey]*TemplInfo` — the value type of `treeMain`, declared at line 447 — whose iteration order Go randomizes per run. I found no sort on that path. One contrast worth noting: the sibling transform in the same file, `handleWithPartial` (function at line 324), hashes the owning template's name into its identifier at line 335 — `hashing.XxHashFromStringHexEncoded(c.t.Name() + withNodeInnerString)` — while the older defer path does not. I checked the implicated files at v0.164.0, v0.165.0 and master `7b5199fdeff7d7682e9f979f468d55bc7b67b934`: `tpl/tplimpl/templatestore.go`, `tpl/templates/templates.go` and `tpl/template.go` are byte-identical at all three, and `tpl/tplimpl/templatetransform.go` differs at master only outside this path — the `handleWith` lines quoted above are unchanged there, at 405-414. ### A constraint on any fix Hashing the owning template's name into the deferred identifier, the way `handleWithPartial` does, would break something the documentation promises for `key`: "This will, combined with a hash of the template content, be used as a cache key." Two *different layouts of the same output format* with identical bodies and one shared key share a single execution today, and that is worth keeping — at both versions, on a variant of the site above reduced to one output format and with the `page` kind enabled plus one content file, so that `single.html` renders at all, I measured a single `DEFER-EXEC-1` for a `home.html` and a `single.html` written that way, with both pages publishing the shared result. Separating registrations by the property that actually differs here — the owner's `IsPlainText`, or its output format — would fix the escaping while leaving that documented same-format sharing untouched. ### Related, not duplicates - #7774, fixed by #8462 ("Fixes #7774", merged 2021-04-23): per-build nondeterminism in output-format template lookup for shortcodes. Same failure shape, different subsystem, and it predates `templates.Defer`. - #13236: two empty deferred blocks *in the same template* collided on the identifier `__hdeferred/cafc7706cee4572b` and panicked; closed as completed. That is the same body-only identifier, in a different situation — the collision there is inside one template, and the cross-output-format escaping consequence does not come up. I did not find an existing report covering byte-identical `templates.Defer` bodies across output formats. ### What I did not establish - **Which registration wins in any individual build.** I inferred the winner from the escaping in the published output; I did not instrument the running binary to observe the registration. - **Platform generality.** Everything above was measured on one machine, Windows 11, amd64 extended builds. Whether the split differs on another platform or core count is unmeasured. - **Two non-plain-text formats sharing a body.** The escaping observable needs an `isPlainText` format paired with an HTML one, so two HTML-ish formats sharing a body were not tested and the reach across format combinations is unknown.

title: hugo mod npm pack emits a publishable, checkout-named package.json

judge.reasoning:
Both patches add `"private": true` and drop the checkout-derived name, so both address the core issue. They differ on the default name and on how they treat existing files.

Patch A uses a fixed, scoped name, `@gohugoio/hugoautogen`. This matches the issue's stated ideal: a scoped name can only be claimed by the scope owner. It always regenerates the field deterministically, so every clone produces the same name and private flag.

Patch B has three problems:
- **Bare default name.** It uses `hugoautogen`, which the issue explicitly warns can be claimed on the registry by anyone.
- **It keeps the bug alive in existing repos.** It reads and preserves `name`, `version` and `private` from any existing generated file. Sites that already committed a manifest from an older Hugo carry checkout-derived names like `site-a`, and Patch B keeps that name forever. For those sites the root cause the issue describes is never fixed.
- **It can preserve `"private": false`.** That partly undermines the do-not-publish guarantee, and it adds read-before-write behavior the issue did not ask for.

Both patches update the existing golden testscripts consistently. Patch A also adds a dedicated testscript asserting the name is not checkout-derived, plus an integration test that parses the JSON properly. Patch B's test relies on string matching and mostly exercises its extra preservation feature.

Patch A is the simpler, more robust fix and aligns more closely with the issue's expectations.

issue_md:
**TL;DR**: the generated `package.json` has no `"private": true` and a checkout-derived `name`, so committed copies are publishable under names sites don't control. Suggested fix: emit `"private": true` and a stable (ideally scoped) default name.

### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)?

```
hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (transcript below is v0.165.0). The behavior is in master's [package_builder.go](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/modules/npm/package_builder.go).

### What happened

`hugo mod npm pack` writes `packages/hugoautogen/package.json` with:

- a **name derived from the checkout directory**, so it varies per clone and can be a registry name the site doesn't control, and
- **no `"private": true`**, npm's do-not-publish guard for internal packages.

The file is regenerated wholesale on each run, so hand-set fields don't survive. From a fresh clone of a repo whose committed copy was hand-normalized:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/google/docsy-example.git site-a && cd site-a
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "@docsy/hugoautogen",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true
$ hugo mod npm pack
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "site-a",
  "version": "0.1.0"
```

A sibling clone of the same repo into `site-b` yields `"name": "site-b"`.

### Why it matters

Sites that commit the generated workspace (e.g. so `npm ci` works without running Hugo first) end up carrying a manifest that npm workspace publishing and common release tools treat as publishable by default: `npm publish --dry-run --workspaces` packs it as `site-a@0.1.0`, while with `"private": true` npm skips the workspace. The name variance also churns the committed manifest, and the lockfile's workspace entry, across differently named checkouts.

### What did you expect

The generated internal workspace is non-publishable (`"private": true`) and has a stable, project-controlled default name rather than the checkout directory's basename. Ideally the default is scoped: a bare name can be claimed on the registry by anyone, a scoped one only by the scope owner.

### Workaround

[docsy-example#487](https://github.com/google/docsy-example/pull/487) follows each pack invocation with a single `npm pkg set` line restoring a scoped name and `private`.

Happy to send a PR for the `private` field (and for the name default, if you have a preference for what it should be).

title: Consider bumping mainImageVersionNumber

judge.reasoning:
Patch A is the better fix: it bumps the version number the issue names and fixes the reason a bump alone would not reach filtered images.

**Correctness.** The issue asks to bump `mainImageVersionNumber` so cached output from two filter-related fixes is invalidated. Before either patch, `Filter()` set `confMain.Key = hashing.HashString(gfilters)` with no version number in it. So bumping `mainImageVersionNumber` by itself would not invalidate filtered images, which are exactly the ones affected by those fixes.
- Patch A handles this cleanly. It moves the version-number assembly into a `versionOptions()` helper and adds an `ImageConfig.FilterKey` method that folds those numbers into the filter cache key. It then bumps `mainImageVersionNumber` to 2. Every cached image, filtered or processed, is invalidated, which is what the issue asks for.
- Patch B also folds the version numbers into the filter key, so filtered images get new hashes. However, it does not bump `mainImageVersionNumber`. Instead it adds a `PNG: 1` format version, which invalidates PNG resizes in a fairly arbitrary way. Its main-version invalidation of filters is only a side effect of changing the hash input.

**Tests.** Patch A adds `TestImageConfigMainVersionNumber`. It checks directly that bumping the main version changes both the processing key and the filter key, a meaningful regression test for the root cause. Patch A also updates all the affected golden hashes and golden image files consistently. Patch B only updates hash expectations and adds no targeted test.

**Scope and craft.** Patch B exports two package-level mutable variables (`MainImageVersionNumber`, `FormatVersionNumbers`), widening the public API, so the filter-key logic can be built inline in `image.go`. That duplicates logic already in `DecodeImageConfig`. Its diff also carries a lot of unrelated reformatting of `AssertFileContent(` calls across test files, which obscures the actual change. Patch A keeps the logic encapsulated in the `images` package, keeps one source for the version options, and stays focused.

issue_md:
Unless site owners flush their image cache, they will not see the result of these fixes:

9e7c978e6 resources/images: Preserve the source palette for geometric filter chains
77856683d resources/images: Fix filters on transparent colors and paletted images

Argument against doing this:  I suspect very few sites are affected by the underlying issues. 

I don't have a strong opinion either way.

title: Bump fileCacheEntryVersion in transform.ToMath

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix: they bump fileCacheEntryVersion from "v1" to "v2" in transform.ToMath. Old cached KaTeX 0.16.21 output then sits under a different key and is no longer reused, which is the root cause in the issue. So both are equally correct.

B adds a comment next to katexVersion in internal/warpc/katex.go telling future upgraders to bump the cache version, and expands the inline comment on the constant. That small craft gain targets exactly how this bug happened (a KaTeX bump without a cache bump).

B also adds an integration test that seeds a stale v1 cache entry and asserts it isn't served. My confidence in this test is limited. Hugo may resolve `caches.misc.dir` as the cache root itself rather than `<dir>/filecache/misc`. If so, the seeded file would never be read, and the test could pass even without the fix. Still, the intent is right, and it adds no risk to production code.

The test's value is uncertain, but B carries the identical fix plus useful guidance to prevent a repeat, so it edges out A.

title: Improve/document security.http.urls override behavior

judge.reasoning: The issue asks for better visibility and documentation of how the security.http.urls override disables the dial-time resolved-address check. Patch B targets that ask directly. It adds a dedicated docs section explaining the behavior, its caveats (permissive allowlists, deny-only lists, repeating defaults plus additions), and a narrow-allowlist recommendation. It also factors the condition into IsResolvedHTTPAddressCheckEnabled with a clear doc comment and adds a hint to AccessDeniedError, so users who hit the denial learn why and how to opt out. Its tests cover the enabled and disabled cases across several custom policies, including the default patterns plus an addition, and assert the new error message. Those tests would fail before the change, since the method and hint don't exist yet. Patch A adds a short doc paragraph about the override, which partly answers the issue. Most of the patch, though, is an unrelated new feature: proxyFromEnvironment, with a custom proxyTransport, context-carried proxy URLs, a reimplemented canonicalAddr, and a new golang.org/x/net dependency. It also changes default behavior by setting base.Proxy = nil, so environment proxies, which were honored before via the cloned DefaultTransport, are now ignored unless the user opts in. That is a regression risk for existing users behind proxies. The added complexity (address matching to bypass the check for the proxy dial) adds risk and obscures the documentation fix the issue asked for. B is focused, lower-risk, better tested for the issue's concern, and improves user-facing diagnostics.

issue_md:
In d6e6f9e500eebdeae8e28de830fff2e3bfc7d534 (unreleased) we added a dial-time URL validation to catch URLs that's valid according to the whitelist but that resolves to a loopback, private or link-local IP addresses. That check is skipped it if the user has a custom `security.http.urls` setup, as it would not make sense to block local development servers.

See `CheckAllowedHTTPAddress`.

This has been reported by @Reload3d  as a potential security issue, and while I think the current behaviour is the pragmatic correct approach, I'm creating this issue for visibility and to see if this can be improved further (e.g. better documentation).

+## Remote URLs and internal addresses
+
+The `http.urls` allowlist only inspects the text of the URL. A hostname that looks harmless can still resolve to an internal address, for example a loopback address (`127.0.0.1`), a private network address (`10.0.0.1`), or the link-local cloud metadata endpoint (`169.254.169.254`).
+

+

+- A permissive allowlist such as `['.*']`, or one composed entirely of deny rules such as the [negation example](#negation-rules) above, lets a hostname that resolves to an internal address through.
+- Repeating the default patterns and adding your own still counts as a custom allowlist.
+
+If you build untrusted content, or build on a machine with access to sensitive internal services (for example, a cloud CI runner with a metadata endpoint), keep the default allowlist or make your custom allowlist as narrow as possible, preferably listing only the exact hosts you need:

+[security.http]

title: Add config option security.http.proxyFromEnvironment = false

judge.reasoning:
Both patches add the `security.http.proxyFromEnvironment` flag, default false, with matching config, docs and TOML test updates. When the flag is off, both set `base.Proxy = nil`, which closes the bypass the issue describes. They differ in what happens when a user opts in.

Patch B sets `base.Proxy = http.ProxyFromEnvironment` and keeps the address-validating dialer for every dial, including the dial to the proxy itself. Proxies usually sit on loopback or a private network address (corporate proxies, local CI proxies). The dial-time check rejects such addresses under the default policy, so the opt-in fails in the common case. Users would have to also loosen `http.urls` (which disables the validation entirely) to make it work.

Patch A handles this properly:
- It resolves the proxy per request via `httpproxy.FromEnvironment` and stores it in the request context.
- It skips the address check only when the dialed address equals the canonical address of the chosen proxy.
- Direct dials, including direct requests to the proxy's own address, still go through the secure dialer.

This makes the opt-in usable without weakening validation for non-proxied traffic, which is the trust model the issue implies: opting in means trusting the proxy.

On tests, Patch A is behavioral. It uses real httptest proxy and target servers and checks three things:
- With the flag off, the proxy is ignored.
- With the flag on, a loopback proxy is used under the hardened default policy.
- Direct loopback destinations, including the proxy's own address, are still denied.

Patch B's test only checks whether `tr.Proxy` is nil or non-nil. It would catch the regression, but it does not exercise behavior and would not reveal the broken opt-in.

Patch A is more complex: a wrapper RoundTripper, a context key, and a `canonicalAddr` that mirrors net/http. That adds some maintenance risk, but the code is well commented and the extra logic is directly tied to making the feature correct. Patch A also adds useful docs on the address validation. Overall Patch A is the more correct and better-tested fix.

issue_md:
This is a security hardening issue.

In d6e6f9e500eebdeae8e28de830fff2e3bfc7d534 (unreleased) we added a dial-time URL validation.

If proxied (e.g. `HTTPS_PROXY` set on users machine or in CI) the above validation will only see the proxy address. There's no workaround for that, but I suggest by adding a new `security.http.proxyFromEnvironment` bool config flag (default disabled).

Thanks to @Reload3d for reporting this issue.

title: js.Build should support es2025 as target

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core fix: they add "es2025": api.ES2025 to the target map in internal/js/esbuild/options.go. That resolves the 'unsupported target: [es2025]' error at its root. Both also extend the TestToBuildOptionsTarget unit table with es2024 and es2025 cases, which would fail before the change and pass after it. Patch A goes further in ways that serve the issue's stated ask. The issue says Hugo doesn't 'support and/or list es2025', and A updates the user-facing docs (options.md) so es2025 appears in the list of valid targets. A also fixes the stale Go doc comment on the Target field, which only listed versions up to es2020. Finally, A adds an end-to-end integration test that mirrors the issue's reproduction: js.Build on a .ts file with minify, sourceMap none and target es2025. That test also checks that an uppercase 'ES2025' is accepted. Asserting exact minified output is somewhat brittle, but it reasonably exercises the reported scenario. The correctness is identical, so A wins on more complete coverage of the issue (documentation listing) and stronger tests, with no added risk.

title: tpl/collections: union silently returns an empty list when the two slice types differ

judge.reasoning:
The issue is that `union` silently returns an empty slice when the two slice types differ. It asks for either a real union or an error.

Patch A replaces the early `return ins.r.Interface(), nil` with an explicit error naming both types. That removes the silent-empty behaviour in every case the issue lists: int/float, int/string, the mixed numeric lists, and `union (slice (slice 1)) (slice 2)`, which previously skipped the uncomparable check. Its tests cover all of these at two levels: unit tests in `TestUnion`, updating the old cases that encoded the buggy `[]string{}` / `[]int{}` results, and an integration test through real templates. It also confirms that same-type and interface-element cases still work (`[1 2]|[1 x]`). It updates the doc comment and the user docs to match.

Patch B only unifies numeric element types. For any non-numeric mismatch it keeps the original `return ins.r.Interface(), nil`, so `union (slice 1) (slice "a")` still silently returns `[]`, and so does the slice-of-slices case. That is exactly the behaviour the issue reports, so B fixes only part of it. B also needed an extra `AssignableTo` guard to handle a prototype-type quirk, which hints at fragility in that path. Its tests cover only the numeric cases and leave the silent-empty expectations for string/int in place.

B matches `intersect` more closely for numbers, but A resolves the root complaint (silent failure) completely and consistently, with stronger tests.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.166.0-DEV-ae07063fcc9a59c95838e83e7fdf12e326ebee7d darwin/arm64
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? I built `master` at `ae07063` and reproduced it there. I did not run a tagged release binary, so I have not confirmed it against one directly, though `Union` is unchanged in `tpl/collections/collections.go`. ### What did you expect to see? `union` either returning the union of its two arguments, or returning an error. It already errors for the other argument shapes it cannot handle, for example `union does not support slices or arrays of uncomparable types` and `can't iterate over ...`. ### What did you see instead? `union` returns an empty slice, with no error, whenever the two arguments have different slice types and neither has an interface element type. `layouts/index.html`: ```go-html-template {{ printf "%T" (slice 1) }} {{ printf "%T" (slice 1.0) }} union int,int -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice 2) }} union int,float -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice 1.0) }} union int,string -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice "a") }} union lists -> {{ union (slice 1 2) (slice 2.0 3.0) }} intersect lists -> {{ intersect (slice 1 2) (slice 2.0 3.0) }} ``` Output: ``` []int []float64 union int,int -> [1 2] union int,float -> [] union int,string -> [] union lists -> [] intersect lists -> [2] ``` `intersect` handles the same two mixed-type lists and returns `[2]`, so the sibling functions disagree about whether these arguments are usable at all. The cause is this early return in `Union`: ```go if l1v.Type() != l2v.Type() && l1v.Type().Elem().Kind() != reflect.Interface && l2v.Type().Elem().Kind() != reflect.Interface { return ins.r.Interface(), nil } ``` `ins.r` is the empty slice made just above, so a caller gets an empty list rather than an error. It is reachable from ordinary templates because `slice 1` is `[]int` and `slice 1.0` is `[]float64`, and it also runs before the uncomparable-types check, so `union (slice (slice 1)) (slice 2)` returns `[]` instead of the error that check would raise. Adding one element of another type to the first argument avoids it, since the slice then becomes `[]interface {}`: `union (slice 1 "x") (slice 1.0)` returns `[1 x]`. ### Stack traceback or browser console output None, no error is raised. That is the problem. --- This is a different mechanism from #3411, which was closed in 2017 and is now locked with a note asking that related bugs be opened as new issues. Happy to send a PR. Returning an error here would be a small change; making `union` accept mixed types the way `intersect` does is bigger, so I would rather you pick the direction first. This issue was written primarily by Claude Code, including the reproduction above.
